# From Devanagari to canonical spelling: the journey of Duryodhana

Long before it became a digital ​address, this name travelled through scripts. **Duryodhana** begins in Devanagari, passes through scholarly transliteration, and arrives in a Latin form that needs no special encoding. Each stage preserves some information ‌and requires some judgment. This post follows that journey: the original evidence, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the material remains, and the reviewed spelling used by the temple.

## At ‌a Glance

- **Restored name:** Duryodhana
- **ASCII form:** duryodhana
- **Meaning:** "'Hard to Conquer in Battle' (dur- 'hard' + yodhana 'fighting') — the eldest Kaurava, rival of the Pāṇḍavas whose refusal to yield ​their share of the kingdom brings about the Kurukṣetra war"
- **Domain of influence:** Ambition, Rivalry, War
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** दुर्योधन (Devanagari)

## Overview

**Duryodhana** (*duryodhana*) — Hard ​to Conquer in Battle · 'Hard to Conquer in Battle' — belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Ambition, Rivalry, War". The name means "'Hard ​to Conquer in Battle' (dur- 'hard' + yodhana 'fighting') — the eldest Kaurava, rival of the Pāṇḍavas whose refusal to yield their share of the kingdom brings about the Kurukṣetra ​war".

**Duryodhana** is the Mahābhārata’s tragic antagonist: the eldest of the hundred Kauravas, peerless mace-fighter, generous friend, and the man whose refusal to yield an inch of the kingdom brought the ​world to war. The epic refuses to make him a villain simple enough to hate — his claim is legally arguable, his grievance real, and his end the war’s most ‌earned lamentation.

PuniCodex records the canonical scholarly spelling **Duryodhana** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/duryodhana/). The displayed form is ASCII-equivalent — a description computed from the displayed form itself. ​The plain ASCII form *duryodhana* contains the same letters: no recovered diacritics or special encoding is claimed. The work here is consistent citation, capitalization, provenance, and cultural context.

## The Name

The ​name is attested in Devanagari as **दुर्योधन**. Etymologically it means "'Hard to Conquer in Battle' (dur- 'hard' + yodhana 'fighting') — the eldest Kaurava, rival of the Pāṇḍavas whose refusal ‌to yield their share of the kingdom brings about the Kurukṣetra war".

The canonical spelling **Duryodhana** matches the conventional scholarly romanization. The plain ASCII form *duryodhana* contains the same letters, ​so no lost diacritics or encoding transition is claimed. The editorial work is to fix one reviewed reference spelling, preserve capitalization and provenance, and keep the original evidence visible. The ‌displayed form is ASCII-equivalent — a description computed from the displayed form itself.

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Devanagari as **दुर्योधन**.

The scholarly transliteration is *Duryodhana*.

The rendering proceeds ​step by step:

- Sanskrit Duryodhana is written in Devanagari as दुर्योधन
- IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots ​beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/dʊrjˈoːdʰənə/** — Sanskrit (IAST: Duryodhana).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Dur-** — The prefix dur- ​means “hard, ill” — the same intensifier as in “duress”.
- **-yo-** — From yudh, “fight”: yodhana, “fighting”. The compound is transparent: hard to conquer in battle.
- **-dhana** — The dh ​is a voiced aspirate; the name his mother chose against his father’s better judgement.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: “door-YO-dhun-uh”

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Birth-name** ​— Suyodhana — “good in battle”; the name was changed by the Pāṇḍavas’ jibe
- **Father** — Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the blind king

He was born Suyodhana; the jeering name by which history ‌knows him is itself a piece of the epic’s blame-work.

## Mythology

Duryodhana’s mythology is the Mahābhārata read from the losing side: the crown prince displaced by cousins the law favoured, ​the commander whose every general was better than his cause. The epic gives him the war’s best exit-line and its most human griefs — for Karṇa, for his sons, and ‌for the pride he would not trade for peace.

### The Ball of Flesh (Ādi Parvan)

Gandhārī carried her pregnancy two years; delivered of a hard mass of flesh, she was about ​to cast it away when Vyāsa ordered it divided — a hundred pieces in oil-jars, and one more that became Duhśalā. Duryodhana’s birth-omen — braying donkeys, circling vultures — had ‌the elders counselling his abandonment; Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s love overruled the omen, and the epic marks the moment the world’s fate turned.

### The Dice Game (Sabhā Parvan)

At Śakuni’s loaded board, Duryodhana ​won the Pāṇḍavas’ kingdom, their liberty, and their queen — and ordered Duḥśāsana to drag Draupadī to the court. Her question — what did you stake first, the kingdom or me? ‌— unmade his legal victory and made his moral one: he returned the stakes and later the kingdom, but the insult outlived the restitution.

### The Embassies and the Refusal (Udyoga ​Parvan)

Krishna came in peace, then as war-herald; the Pāṇḍavas asked for five villages. ‘I will not give the Pāṇḍavas land equal to the point of a needle’ — Duryodhana’s ‌answer to Krishna’s peace-mission is the epic’s hinge. Every reader who has wished he’d yielded has made the epic’s point: the war was chosen, not fated.

### The Last Duel (Śalya & ​Bhīma)

On the war’s final day Duryodhana, alone of the hundred, met Bhīma by the lake of blood. Equal until the last, he fell to the mace-blow Bhīma aimed below ​the belt — the one illegal stroke of their duel, urged by Krishna. The epic lets the ‘good’ side win by the foul its cause had licensed; Duryodhana’s dying reproach ‌stands unanswered in the text.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Duryodhana concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The Hundredth ‌Son** — Born of Gandhārī’s split pregnancy as a ball of flesh, divided into a hundred sons by Vyāsa’s grace.
- **Mace-Master** — The equal of Bhīma with the gadā; his duel ‌with Bhīma closes the war’s eighteenth day.
- **Friend of Karṇa** — The epic’s one unbreakable friendship: the outcast-sūta king he crowned against all caste law.
- **The Dice Refusal** — “Not ​a needle’s point of land” — the sentence that made the Kurukṣetra war inevitable.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material record for Duryodhana survives in a small number of securely identified ​remains, catalogued below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

Duryodhana’s monuments are performance: the Kutiyattam and Kathakali stages of Kerala ‌keep the dice-game and the embassies in living repertory; and the Indonesian wayang kulit shadow-theatre’s Duryudana puppets are museum-pieces of the epic’s longest journey.

## Across Cultures

Duryodhana is the epic’s dark mirror of the dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira: where the eldest Pāṇḍava keeps the letter ‌and loses the spirit, Duryodhana keeps the pride and loses everything. Later tradition made him a byword for envy, but the critical readings — from the Bhārata’s own ambivalence to modern ​novelists — keep restoring the man the epic refused to flatten.

Within the Sanskrit tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[aditi|Aditi]], [[agni|Agni]], [[ambika|Ambikā]], [[amsa|Aṃśa]], [[arjuna|Arjuna]], and [[bhakti|Bhakti]].

## Cultural ‌Legacy

His name is the subcontinent’s standing word for ruinous obstinacy; his friendship with Karṇa, for loyalty across caste. The dice-game is staged as dance-drama across South and Southeast Asia; ​and in Indonesian wayang, where the Mahābhārata became a national epic, Duryodhana (Duryudana) is among the most beloved characters — the loser the culture refuses to disown.

## A ​Meditation

Duryodhana: a name that means “hard to conquer”, worn by the man history conquered most completely. Restored plainly, it keeps its double edge — the boast and the epitaph ‌in four syllables, the epic’s whole tragedy compressed into one who would not yield a needle’s point.
